transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Kenji Watanabe (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Head of ML - Mariner), Tom Brooks (CTO), Lena Ortiz (Platform Eng)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Sofia from Redwood. With me is Kenji our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Priya: Doing well, thanks. Appreciate you making time. We've been looking at options to move off OpenAI for cost reasons and some data residency asks.
[00:12] Tom: Yeah, hi all. High level  we run a customer-facing chat assistant, about ~120 qps at peak across 3 regions, most requests are short, but we do a lot of multi-turn context. Latency is pretty important for UX.
[00:25] Kenji: Great, that's helpful. So goal today is to understand your current stack, constraints, and what migration parity looks like for you. Can you give a quick run through of current infra?
[00:33] Priya: Sure. Today we use OpenAI's chat endpoint for our assistant, a mixture of gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini for cheaper flows. We also run an internal vLLM-based service for some batch re-ranking and embeddings using TGI for local infra experiments. Tokenization and prompt engineering is pretty tuned to the OpenAI models.
[00:48] Lena: On infra side, we normally host in Azure, want to keep data regionally isolated (EU for EU customers). We're evaluating Dedicated because the committed capacity model fits our predictable load and gives us control over logs/data.
[01:02] Sofia: Makes sense. A few common concerns we've seen: eval parity (does the model output match your current baseline), latency SLOs on Dedicated, integration work for tokenization and tool calling, and security controls like KMS, SSO/SAML, audit logs. We can walk through each.
[01:16] Tom: For eval parity  the business can't tolerate big regressions. We have an eval dataset of ~5k prompts. We want Redwood to run a parity benchmark vs OpenAI and show comparable responses per our scoring. Also curious about vLLM behavior  we currently use vLLM for lower-cost inference, any differences there?
[01:33] Kenji: Totally. For parity we recommend a three-step benchmark: (1) run your eval set against OpenAI baseline we both agree on, (2) run same set against Redwood-hosted and Dedicated variants (model pins), and (3) run side-by-side scoring including regression alerts. We can include TGI/vLLM as additional comparators if you want. Note: tokenization differences can cause small divergence, we'll capture that in the scoring.
[01:54] Priya: What's the delta typically? Like how often are outputs materially different? We need a threshold for acceptance.
[02:00] Kenji: It depends on model variant. If you're moving to an identical open model (same weights) differences are mostly tokenizer and decoding-sampling seeds. If you're moving to a Redwood-verified variant or quantized model for Dedicated, differences can appear in longer, factual answers or when the model's temperature/bias differs. In our experience teams accept 95% parity on top-n similarity metrics and ask manual review on the problematic 5%.
[02:23] Tom: That 95% sounds reasonable as a starting point. We also care about latency. Our SLO is 250ms P95 for short prompts under 128 tokens. How does Redwood Dedicated typically perform?
[02:35] Kenji: On Dedicated with A100-class nodes and our optimized runtime, for short sequences we've seen 80-160ms P95 when batching is small and KV cache is used. For multi-turn large contexts latency increases; we use prefix caching to mitigate. Obviously results depend on model size. For gpt-4o-like families numbers vary.
[02:53] Lena: We're also running vLLM for some workloads because it's cheap, but ops overhead is high. Can Redwood Dedicated replace that or would we still need vLLM for selective routes?
[03:04] Sofia: Many customers keep vLLM for ad-hoc experiments but migrate production routes to Dedicated because you get predictable throughput, SLA and simpler ops. Redwood also supports autoscaling and burst capacity so you don't have to manage the lower-level runtime yourself.
[03:16] Priya: Security: do you support customer-managed KMS and HSM? We need to ensure encryption keys never leave our cloud env.
[03:22] Kenji: Yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM. For Dedicated we offer integration with customer KMS for key wrapping and audit logs; we'll share the security playbook. Also SOC2 report available.
[03:34] Tom: Any compliance experience with Azure regions and VNet peering?
[03:37] Kenji: Yes, Dedicated can be deployed in Azure with VNet peering for Private-style controls. For full air-gapped on-prem you might look at our Private offering; Dedicated sits between hosted and private in terms of isolation.
[03:49] Priya: On the topic of integration  we have an existing prompt engineering layer and a tool call orchestration system. How much work to switch endpoints? Are there breaking changes in tokenization, tool calls (function calling) or rate limits?
[04:03] Kenji: We provide API compatibility layers for common endpoints. Function/tool calling is supported; payload formats are similar but not identical  you'll need small adapter changes. Tokenizer differences are minor but important for cost accounting; we'll help with a tokenizer mapping and cost delta estimates. Rate limit patterns can be tuned with our quotas and dedicated capacity avoids noisy neighbor rate throttling.
[04:22] Lena: Cost  rough ballpark for Dedicated? We're thinking 4 GPUs to start (predictable).
[04:27] Sofia: We'll send a detailed pricing sheet, but ballpark for a 4x A100 Dedicated cluster is in the low-mid tens of thousands per month depending on commit and term. Kenji: worth noting unit cost per token usually goes down with batching and our KV/prefix cache; we'll show cost optimization suggestions.
[04:43] Priya: About eval: we run both automatic and human evaluation. Can you preserve exact request/response logs for reproducibility?
[04:50] Kenji: Yes, Dedicated can persist request/response logs to your storage; we also support export for audit. For Hosted we retain less long-term by default.
[04:58] Tom: Any gotchas moving from OpenAI to an OSS model family? We tried TGI/vLLM and saw hallucination drift in some templates.
[05:05] Kenji: Switching model families can surface generalization differences; that's why we recommend model-level A/B tests. Redwood's model catalog includes verified performance profiles and recommended quantization settings. We can also pin to model versions to make rollouts deterministic.
[05:20] Priya: For our pilot, we want to test 3 endpoints: chat for the assistant, a re-ranker batch job, and embeddings for semantic search. Can Redwood run all three on Dedicated?
[05:29] Sofia: Yep. Dedicated supports multiple routes and models pinned per route. You can assign throughput partitions so embeddings jobs don't starve chat.
[05:36] Lena: Who will own the pilot setup? We prefer Redwood to run the benchmark but we'll provide eval data and scoring script.
[05:42] Kenji: We'll own provisioning and initial runs; we ask you to provide the eval set, scoring keys and any baseline thresholds. We'll produce a benchmark report with regression highlights.
[05:53] Priya: Timeline: we want to decide within 2 weeks. Can you do a benchmark and have results in one week?
[05:58] Kenji: Yes, if you share the eval set and access by end of week we can run a parity benchmark and share results within 5 business days.
[06:05] Tom: Any legal/procurement blockers  we need standard contract clauses for data residency and indemnity.
[06:11] Sofia: We'll share our standard Dedicated contract template and can flag any negotiated clauses. Procurement often wants DPA + security addendum; we'll attach those.
[06:18] Priya: One last thing  how do you handle model updates? If Redwood updates a model that changes outputs, what's the rollback story?
[06:24] Kenji: You can pin routes to model versions. For hosted we do versioned rollouts; for Dedicated you control the pinned binaries and we support canary rollouts and automatic fallbacks to previous model variants. We'll add that to the replay documentation.
[06:36] Tom: Great. I wanted to ask about token counting differences; our billing is token based so any mismatch causes accounting headaches.
[06:42] Kenji: We'll provide tokenizer mapping and a delta report so you can adjust budgets. Also Redwood Console includes token-level cost breakdowns per route.
[06:51] Lena: Ok, that sounds useful.
[06:54] Sofia: Recap  action items: Sofia sends SOC2 + security playbook + pricing; Kenji runs parity benchmark once Priya shares eval data; Priya shares the eval prompts and sample traffic; follow-up meeting to review results.
[07:06] Priya: Sounds good. We might want to include a product manager and procurement in the next call.
[07:10] Sofia: Absolutely. We'll propose times after Kenji shares results. Thanks everyone.

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had occasional name mislabels (Tom/Tom\u00e1s) and engine names (v-L-L-M vs vLLM), some punctuation dropped. Partial cross-talk around 00:48-01:04.

End of meeting.
